The tilt of a key depends on $(p,q)$ only through the prime ratio $r = q/p$, via
$z(r) = (r^{-1/2}-2^{-1/2})/(1-2^{-1/2})$, so the winner is a property of the key-generation
law and not of any individual key.  The two orders tie at the critical ratio
$r^\star = 24 - 16\sqrt{2} = 1.372583\ldots$, strictly inside the balance band $(1,2)$:
enforcing $q < 2p$ does not determine the winner.  A ratio-uniform pool on $[1,2]$ has mean
tilt exactly $\sqrt{2}-1 < 1/2$, favouring ascending by exactly $\sqrt2$.  The deployed class
--- two primes drawn independently and uniformly from the same bit-length window --- has ratio
density $f(r) = 4/r^{2}-1$ on $[1,2]$, obtained by differentiating the exact planar area
$A(r) = 5/2 - 2/r - r/2$; its mean tilt is exactly $(9-5\sqrt2)/3 = 0.642977\ldots > 1/2$, with
tilt-only speedup $(5\sqrt2-6)/(9-5\sqrt2) = 0.555265\ldots$: window-ascending \emph{loses}
about $44\%$ of the work, and $5 - 4/r^\star - r^\star \approx 0.7132$ of individual keys are
won by descending.  Inside the one-parameter family with density proportional to $r^{-\theta}$ on $[1,2]$ the
mean tilt is strictly increasing in $\theta$ and crosses $1/2$ at exactly $\theta^\star = 3/2$.
No window redesign repairs this: for multiplier $R>1$ the tie ratio is
$4R/(1+\sqrt R)^2 \in (1, \min(R,4))$, and ratio-uniform pools on $[1,R]$ have mean tilt
$1/(1+\sqrt R) < 1/2$ always.  A half-step margin criterion transfers the continuum comparison
to the true integer window.  The conclusion is a scoped negative result: the window-ascending
advantage is confined to artificially ratio-spread populations and is adversarially reversed on
those deployed generators actually produce.  No factoring speedup is claimed or implied.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} semiprime factorisation; divisor scan order; prime ratio law;
generator tilt; canonical balance window; closed-form mean tilt; no-go theorem.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The question}

Let $N = pq$ be a semiprime with $p \le q$.  Trial division for the small factor need only test
integers up to $\sqrt N$.  If in addition the factorisation is \emph{balanced}, i.e.\ $q < 2p$,
then $p^2 \le N < 2p^2$ and hence
\[
  \sqrt{N/2} < p \le \sqrt N,
\]
so the search may be confined to the \textbf{canonical window}
$W(N) = (\sqrt{N/2},\,\sqrt N]$, of length $(1-2^{-1/2})\sqrt N \approx 0.2929\sqrt N$.

Confining the search leaves a free choice: the traversal order.  Two orders are canonical.
\emph{Window-ascending} starts at the bottom and increases, costing $d-a+1$ touches to reach a
divisor $d$ in a window with lower end $a$; \emph{sqrt-descending} starts at
$\lfloor \sqrt N \rfloor$ and decreases, costing $b-d+1$.  Which is cheaper, and on which
populations of keys?

This is a \emph{reorder-class} question: neither scan changes the asymptotic complexity of
trial division.  But the constant factor has a clean and complete answer, and that answer says
something structural about the interaction between an algorithm and the population it is
benchmarked on.

\subsection{The claim under test}

An empirical claim held that window-ascending enjoys a systematic advantage over
sqrt-descending on balanced semiprimes, with synthetic pools reporting speedups near
$1.5$--$1.6$ in favour of ascending.  We show the claim is correct on the pools where it was
measured and \emph{false, with the opposite sign and comparable magnitude}, on the pools that
deployed key generators actually produce.  The reversal is not an empirical accident: both
regimes are computed here in closed form, and the two closed forms lie on opposite sides of the
decision threshold.

\subsection{Contributions}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Reduction to one scalar} (\S\ref{sec:reduction}): the pool comparison is decided
        by the mean tilt alone, with an exact speedup law and explicit predictor error identity.
  \item \textbf{Tilt is a generator property} (\S\ref{sec:generator}): the tilt depends only on
        $r = q/p$; the tie ratio $24-16\sqrt2$ lies strictly inside the balance band.
  \item \textbf{Exact solution of the deployed class} (\S\ref{sec:deployed}): ratio density
        $4/r^2-1$, mean tilt exactly $(9-5\sqrt2)/3 > 1/2$.
  \item \textbf{Window-design no-go} (\S\ref{sec:nogo}).
  \item \textbf{Transfer to integer scans} (\S\ref{sec:integer}).
  \item \textbf{Agreement with measurement} (\S\ref{sec:measure}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Setup and definitions}

Throughout, a \emph{window} is a pair of integers $a \le b$ and a \emph{divisor position} is an
integer $d$ with $a \le d \le b$.

\begin{definition}[Scan costs]
The \textbf{ascending cost} of a scan of $[a,b]$ stopping at $d$ is $\asc(a,d) = d-a+1$; the
\textbf{descending cost} is $\dsc(b,d) = b-d+1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Tilt]
For $a<b$ and $x \in \mathbb R$, the \textbf{tilt} is $t(a,b;x) = (x-a)/(b-a)$.  For a finite
pool $S$ of keys with divisor positions $d_i$ in a common window $[a,b]$, the \textbf{mean
tilt} is $\bar z = |S|^{-1}\sum_{i \in S} t(a,b;d_i)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Pool totals]
$T_{\asc} = \sum_{i\in S}\asc(a,d_i)$ and $T_{\dsc} = \sum_{i\in S}\dsc(b,d_i)$.  The
\textbf{pool speedup} of ascending over descending is $S = T_{\dsc}/T_{\asc}$; a value $>1$
means ascending is cheaper.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Prime ratio and balance]
For $N = pq$ with $0 < p \le q$, the \textbf{prime ratio} is $r = q/p \ge 1$.  The pair is
\textbf{balanced} if $r < 2$; the \textbf{balance band} is $r \in (1,2)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Canonical window, integer form]
$a(N) = \lceil \sqrt{N/2}\,\rceil$ and $b(N) = \lfloor \sqrt N \rfloor$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Window multiplier]
For $R>1$ the $R$-window is $(\sqrt{N/R},\,\sqrt N]$; scanning it upward is well defined
whenever the generator guarantees $q < Rp$.  The canonical window is $R=2$.
\end{definition}

\section{The reduction: one scalar decides the contest}\label{sec:reduction}

\subsection{Conservation of scan budget}

\begin{lemma}[Conservation law]\label{lem:cons}
For all integers $a,b,d$: $\asc(a,d) + \dsc(b,d) = (b-a)+2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$(d-a+1)+(b-d+1) = b-a+2$; the divisor cancels.
\end{proof}

The two orders share a fixed budget: whatever one saves the other spends.  This is the
structural reason the comparison reduces to a location statistic.

\begin{lemma}[Pointwise inversion]\label{lem:point}
$\dsc(b,d) < \asc(a,d)$ if and only if $a+b < 2d$, i.e.\ $d$ lies strictly above the window
midpoint.
\end{lemma}

\subsection{Window membership is exactly balance}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:window}
Let $N = pq$ with positive integers $p,q$.  Then $p^2 \le N < 2p^2$ if and only if $p \le q$ and
$q < 2p$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Cancel the positive factor $p$: $p^2 \le pq \iff p \le q$, and $pq < 2p^2 = p\cdot 2p \iff
q < 2p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Same bit length forces window membership]\label{cor:bitlen}
If $2^{b-1} \le p \le q < 2^{b}$ with $b \ge 1$, then $q < 2^{b} = 2\cdot 2^{b-1} \le 2p$, so
$p^2 \le N < 2p^2$.
\end{corollary}

This matters for the refutation: on a pool of two independent primes of equal bit length, every
key is inside the window, so the ascending scan is always well defined and its loss cannot be
attributed to window misses.

\begin{remark}
Off-balance semiprimes genuinely escape: $21 = 3\cdot 7$ has $9 \le 21$ but $21 \ge 18 =
2\cdot 3^2$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The tilt form of the totals}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:totals}
For a nonempty pool $S$ in a common window with $a<b$ and $L = b-a$,
\[
  T_{\asc} = |S|\,(L\bar z + 1), \qquad T_{\dsc} = |S|\,\bigl(L(1-\bar z)+1\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$T_{\asc} = \sum_i (d_i-a) + |S| = L\sum_i t(a,b;d_i) + |S| = |S|(L\bar z+1)$; the descending
form follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cons} summed over the pool.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact speedup law]\label{thm:speedup}
For a nonempty pool with $a<b$, $L = b-a$ and $\bar z > 0$,
\[
  S \;=\; \frac{T_{\dsc}}{T_{\asc}} \;=\; \frac{L(1-\bar z)+1}{L\bar z+1}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Divide the two expressions of Lemma~\ref{lem:totals}; the pool size cancels and the denominator
is positive.
\end{proof}

No higher moment of the divisor distribution enters: the speedup depends on the population only
through $\bar z$.

\begin{theorem}[Inversion theorem]\label{thm:inversion}
For a nonempty pool with $a<b$: $\;T_{\dsc} < T_{\asc}$ if and only if $\bar z > 1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:totals} the inequality reads $L(1-\bar z)+1 < L\bar z + 1$, i.e.\
$L(1-2\bar z) < 0$, i.e.\ $\bar z > 1/2$ since $L>0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The tilt-only predictor and its exact error}

For large $L$ the speedup law simplifies to the \textbf{tilt-only predictor}
$P(\bar z) = (1-\bar z)/\bar z$.

\begin{proposition}[Error identity]\label{prop:err}
For $L>0$ and $z>0$,
\[
  \frac{L(1-z)+1}{Lz+1} - \frac{1-z}{z} \;=\; \frac{2z-1}{z\,(Lz+1)}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Over the common denominator $z(Lz+1)$ the numerator of the left side is
$z(L(1-z)+1) - (1-z)(Lz+1) = 2z-1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Predictor accuracy]\label{cor:err}
For $0 < z \le 1$ and $L>0$,
$\bigl|\,(L(1-z)+1)/(Lz+1) - (1-z)/z\,\bigr| \le 1/(Lz^{2})$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The modulus equals $|2z-1|/(z(Lz+1)) \le 1/(z\cdot Lz)$, using $|2z-1|\le 1$ and $Lz+1 > Lz$.
\end{proof}

The error vanishes identically at $z = 1/2$, so the predictor never misclassifies the winner; it
only misreports the margin.  Since $L = \Theta(\sqrt N)$, at cryptographic sizes it is exact to
more digits than any measurement can resolve.

\section{The tilt is a property of the generator}\label{sec:generator}

\subsection{The ratio law}

\begin{theorem}[Bridge theorem]\label{thm:bridge}
For real $p,q>0$, the normalised height of $p$ inside $(\sqrt{pq/2},\,\sqrt{pq}]$ is
\[
  \frac{p - \sqrt{pq/2}}{\sqrt{pq}-\sqrt{pq/2}} \;=\; z(q/p),
  \qquad z(r) := \frac{r^{-1/2}-2^{-1/2}}{1-2^{-1/2}} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $p = u^2$, $q = v^2$ with $u,v>0$; then $\sqrt{pq} = uv$ and $\sqrt{pq/2} = uv/\sqrt2$, so
dividing numerator and denominator by $uv$ gives $(u/v - 1/\sqrt2)/(1 - 1/\sqrt2)$.  Since
$\sqrt{q/p} = v/u$, we have $u/v = (q/p)^{-1/2}$.
\end{proof}

The size of $N$ has cancelled: the tilt is scale-free, a function of the ratio alone.  The
scan-order winner is thus determined by the \emph{law of the prime ratio} emitted by a
generator.  We call $\bar z = \E[z(r)]$ the \textbf{generator tilt}.

\begin{proposition}[Monotonicity and endpoints]\label{prop:mono}
$z$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, with $z(1) = 1$ and $z(2) = 0$.
\end{proposition}

Perfectly balanced keys sit at the \emph{top} of the window and maximally unbalanced ones at the
bottom.  This is the geometric content of the inversion: balance pushes the small factor toward
$\sqrt N$, exactly where the descending scan begins.

\subsection{The critical ratio}

\begin{theorem}[Tie ratio]\label{thm:tie}
Let $r^\star = 24 - 16\sqrt2$.  Then $z(r^\star) = 1/2$ and, for $r>0$,
$z(r) > 1/2 \iff r < r^\star$.  Moreover $1 < r^\star < 2$, with
$r^\star = 1.3725830\ldots$
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\sqrt{r^\star} = 4-2\sqrt2$, since $(4-2\sqrt2)^2 = 16-16\sqrt2+8 = 24-16\sqrt2$ and
$4-2\sqrt2>0$.  Using $(4-2\sqrt2)(4+2\sqrt2) = 8$,
\[
  z(r^\star) = \frac{\frac{4+2\sqrt2}{8}-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt2-1}{\sqrt2}} = \frac12 .
\]
The equivalence follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:mono}; the bracketing from
$1.41421 < \sqrt2 < 1.41422$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Balance is not sufficient]\label{cor:balance}
The dividing line lies strictly inside the balance band.  A generator enforcing $q < 2p$ ---
exactly what makes the ascending scan well defined --- has thereby determined \emph{nothing}
about which order wins.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The hard-balance control pool}

\begin{theorem}[Ratio-uniform mean tilt]\label{thm:unif}
If the prime ratio is uniform on $[1,2]$ then
$\bar z = \int_1^2 z(r)\,dr = \sqrt2 - 1 = 0.4142135\ldots$
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\int_1^2 r^{-1/2}dr = 2\sqrt2-2$, so with $c = 2^{-1/2}$,
\[
  \int_1^2 z = \frac{(2\sqrt2-2)-c}{1-c}
             = \frac{\sqrt2(2\sqrt2-2)-1}{\sqrt2-1}
             = \frac{3-2\sqrt2}{\sqrt2-1}
             = \frac{(\sqrt2-1)^2}{\sqrt2-1} = \sqrt2-1 .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:unif}
$\sqrt2-1 < 1/2$: the ratio-uniform pool is bottom-heavy, window-ascending wins, and its
tilt-only speedup is $(2-\sqrt2)/(\sqrt2-1) = \sqrt2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Multiply numerator and denominator by $\sqrt2+1$: $(2-\sqrt2)(\sqrt2+1) = \sqrt2$ and
$(\sqrt2-1)(\sqrt2+1) = 1$.
\end{proof}

\section{The deployed generator class, solved exactly}\label{sec:deployed}

\begin{model}\label{mod:ind}
Let $p,q$ be independent and uniform on $[1,2]$ (the normalisation of a dyadic bit-length window
$[2^{b-1},2^{b})$), conditioned on $p \le q$; let $r = q/p \in [1,2]$.
\end{model}

By Corollary~\ref{cor:bitlen} every such pair lies inside the canonical window.

\subsection{The exact area and the ratio density}

\begin{theorem}[Planar area]\label{thm:area}
For $1 \le r \le 2$, the area of $\{(p,q)\in[1,2]^2 : p \le q \le rp\}$ is
\[
  A(r) \;=\; \int_1^2\bigl(\min(rp,2)-p\bigr)\,dp \;=\; \frac52-\frac2r-\frac r2 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Slice by $p$: the vertical extent above $p$ is $\min(rp,2)-p$, and $rp \le 2$ exactly when
$p \le t := 2/r$, with $1 \le t \le 2$.  Splitting at $t$,
\[
  \int_1^{t}(r-1)p\,dp + \int_{t}^{2}(2-p)\,dp
  = (r-1)\frac{t^2-1}{2} + \Bigl[2p-\tfrac{p^2}{2}\Bigr]_{t}^{2},
\]
which with $t = 2/r$ equals $(r-1)(4/r^2-1)/2 + 2 - 4/r + 2/r^2 = 5/2 - 2/r - r/2$.
\end{proof}

Sanity checks: $A(1)=0$ (no ordered pair has ratio below $1$) and $A(2)=1/2$ (the half-square
$\{p\le q\}$, since every ordered pair from $[1,2]$ has ratio at most $2$).

\begin{theorem}[Ratio density]\label{thm:density}
$A'(r) = 2/r^2 - 1/2 = f(r)/2$ with $f(r) := 4/r^2 - 1$, and $f$ is a probability density on
$[1,2]$.  Moreover, for $s \ge 1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cdf}
  \int_1^{s} f(r)\,dr \;=\; 5 - \frac4s - s .
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The derivative is elementary; the conditioning constant is the total mass $A(2) = 1/2$, so the
density of $r$ is $A'(r)/A(2) = f(r)$.  Nonnegativity on $[1,2]$ is $r \le 2$.  An antiderivative
is $-4/r - r$, giving \eqref{eq:cdf}; at $s=2$ it equals $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Shape]\label{rem:shape}
$f(1) = 3$ and $f(2) = 0$: the density is heaped against perfect balance.  By \eqref{eq:cdf} the
median ratio solves $5 - 4/s - s = 1/2$, giving $s \approx 1.2192$; and $z(5/4) =
0.63955\ldots$, already comfortably above $1/2$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The exact mean tilt}

\begin{theorem}[Main theorem: deployed generator tilt]\label{thm:main}
Under Model~\ref{mod:ind},
\[
  \bar z_{\mathrm{ind}} \;=\; \int_1^2 z(r) f(r)\,dr \;=\; \frac{9-5\sqrt2}{3}
  \;=\; 0.6429773\ldots
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $c = 2^{-1/2}$,
\[
  z(r)f(r) = \frac{1}{1-c}\Bigl(4r^{-5/2} - r^{-1/2} - 4c\,r^{-2} + c\Bigr),
\]
whose bracket has antiderivative
$G(r) = -\tfrac83 r^{-3/2} - 2r^{1/2} + 4c\,r^{-1} + c\,r$, as term-by-term differentiation
confirms.  Evaluating with $c = \sqrt2/2$ gives $G(2) = -2\sqrt2/3$ and
$G(1) = -14/3 + 5\sqrt2/2$, hence
\[
  G(2)-G(1) = \frac{14}{3} - \frac{19\sqrt2}{6}
            = \frac{9-5\sqrt2}{3}\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Bigr).
\]
Dividing by $1-c$ yields the stated value.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Analytic refutation]\label{cor:refute}
$\bar z_{\mathrm{ind}} > 1/2$, since $18 - 10\sqrt2 > 3 \iff \sqrt2 < 1.5$.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:inversion} the sqrt-descending order strictly beats window-ascending on the
deployed class --- as a theorem, with no appeal to simulation.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Exact loss]\label{cor:loss}
The tilt-only speedup of the deployed class is
\[
  P(\bar z_{\mathrm{ind}})
  = \frac{5\sqrt2-6}{9-5\sqrt2} = 0.5552646\ldots,
\]
so window-ascending performs about $1.80$ times as much work as sqrt-descending: it loses
roughly $44\%$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The inversion is typical, not a tail effect}

\begin{theorem}[Per-key frequency]\label{thm:freq}
Under Model~\ref{mod:ind} the probability that a key's ratio falls below the critical ratio ---
equivalently, that sqrt-descending wins on that individual key --- is
\[
  \Prb[r < r^\star] \;=\; 5 - \frac{4}{r^\star} - r^\star \;=\; 0.71320\ldots
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substitute $s = r^\star$ in \eqref{eq:cdf}; the numerical value follows from
$1.37248 < r^\star < 1.37264$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Opposite sides of the tie]\label{cor:sides}
$\sqrt2 - 1 < 1/2 < (9-5\sqrt2)/3$.  The ratio-uniform control pool and the independent
same-bit-length pool land on strictly opposite sides of the decision threshold; this dichotomy
is the entire content of the scope boundary.
\end{corollary}


\subsection{A one-parameter family through the tie}

The two solved classes are two points of a natural interpolating family.  For
$\theta \in \mathbb R$ let $\mu_\theta$ be the law on $[1,2]$ with density proportional to
$r^{-\theta}$; then $\mu_0$ is the ratio-uniform control, and increasing $\theta$ piles mass
against perfect balance, mimicking the deployed concentration.

\begin{theorem}[Exact crossing exponent]\label{thm:theta}
Write $I(s) = \int_1^2 r^{-s}\,dr$.  Then $\E_{\mu_\theta}[z]$ is strictly increasing in
$\theta$, tends to $0$ as $\theta\to-\infty$ and to $1$ as $\theta\to+\infty$, and equals
$1/2$ at the single point $\theta^\star = 3/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $c = 2^{-1/2}$ one has
$\E_{\mu_\theta}[z] = \bigl(I(\theta+\tfrac12)/I(\theta)-c\bigr)/(1-c)$, so the tie condition is
$I(\theta+\tfrac12)/I(\theta) = (1+c)/2$.  At $\theta = 3/2$, $I(2) = 1/2$ and
$I(3/2) = 2-\sqrt2$, so using $(2-\sqrt2)(2+\sqrt2)=2$,
\[
  \frac{I(2)}{I(3/2)} = \frac{1}{2(2-\sqrt2)} = \frac{2+\sqrt2}{4} = \frac{1+c}{2}.
\]
For monotonicity: if $\theta_1<\theta_2$ then $d\mu_{\theta_2}/d\mu_{\theta_1} \propto
r^{-(\theta_2-\theta_1)}$ is strictly decreasing, so $\mu_{\theta_2}$ is stochastically smaller
than $\mu_{\theta_1}$, and $z$ is strictly decreasing by Proposition~\ref{prop:mono}.  The
limits follow because $\mu_\theta$ concentrates at $r=2$ and at $r=1$ respectively.
\end{proof}

A generator whose ratio density decays like $r^{-\theta}$ near balance is therefore adversarial
to the ascending scan exactly when $\theta > 3/2$.

\section{Window design cannot rescue the ascending scan}\label{sec:nogo}

\begin{definition}
The $R$-tilt law is $z_R(r) = (r^{-1/2}-R^{-1/2})/(1-R^{-1/2})$; the canonical case is $z_2 = z$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[General tie ratio]\label{thm:tieR}
For $R>1$ put $r^\star(R) = 4R/(1+\sqrt R)^2$.  Then $z_R(r^\star(R)) = 1/2$, $z_R$ is strictly
decreasing, and $z_R(r) > 1/2 \iff r < r^\star(R)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\sqrt{r^\star(R)} = 2\sqrt R/(1+\sqrt R)$, so $r^\star(R)^{-1/2} = \tfrac12(R^{-1/2}+1)$, the
midpoint of $R^{-1/2}$ and $1$; substituting into $z_R$ gives $1/2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No-go bounds]\label{thm:nogo}
For every $R>1$: $\;1 < r^\star(R) < R$ and $r^\star(R) < 4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $s = \sqrt R>1$, so $r^\star = 4s^2/(1+s)^2$.  Then $r^\star>1 \iff 2s>1+s \iff s>1$;
$r^\star<R \iff 4 < (1+s)^2 \iff s>1$; and $r^\star<4 \iff s^2 < (1+s)^2$, immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Design no-go]\label{cor:nogo}
For every $R>1$ there is $r$ with $1 < r < \min(R,4)$ and $z_R(r) > 1/2$: an interval of
near-balanced ratios just above $1$ is adversarial to the ascending scan \emph{for every
window}, and the tie point can never be pushed past ratio $4$.  Since deployed generators
concentrate ratio mass near $1$ (Remark~\ref{rem:shape}), no window design removes the
adversarial tilt.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Take $r = (1+r^\star(R))/2$ and apply Theorems~\ref{thm:tieR} and \ref{thm:nogo}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Ratio-uniform pools are bottom-heavy for every window]\label{thm:unifR}
If $r$ is uniform on $[1,R]$ then
$\frac{1}{R-1}\int_1^{R} z_R(r)\,dr = \frac{1}{1+\sqrt R} < \frac12$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\int_1^R r^{-1/2}dr = 2\sqrt R-2$, so multiplying numerator and denominator by $\sqrt R$,
\[
  \int_1^R z_R
  = \frac{\sqrt R(2\sqrt R-2)-(R-1)}{\sqrt R-1}
  = \frac{R-2\sqrt R+1}{\sqrt R-1}
  = \sqrt R - 1 = \frac{R-1}{1+\sqrt R}.
\]
Dividing by $R-1$ gives $1/(1+\sqrt R) < 1/2$ exactly when $\sqrt R > 1$.
\end{proof}

At $R=2$ this recovers Theorem~\ref{thm:unif}, since $1/(1+\sqrt2) = \sqrt2-1$; and
$r^\star(2) = 8/(3+2\sqrt2) = 8(3-2\sqrt2) = 24-16\sqrt2$ recovers Theorem~\ref{thm:tie}.
Bottom-heaviness is thus a property of ratio-\emph{spread} populations, uniformly across window
designs --- and such populations are laboratory constructions.

\section{From the continuum to the integer scan}\label{sec:integer}

\begin{definition}[Margin]
$m(r) = r^{-1/2} - \tfrac12\bigl(1+2^{-1/2}\bigr)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:margin}
$m(r)>0 \iff z(r) > 1/2 \iff r < r^\star$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$z(r)>1/2$ reads $r^{-1/2}-2^{-1/2} > \tfrac12(1-2^{-1/2})$, i.e.\
$r^{-1/2} > \tfrac12(1+2^{-1/2})$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Half-step transfer]\label{lem:halfstep}
Let $\alpha\le\beta$ be reals and $d$ an integer with $\alpha+\beta+1 \le 2d$.  Then on the
rounded window $[\lceil\alpha\rceil,\lfloor\beta\rfloor]$ we have
$\dsc(\lfloor\beta\rfloor,d) < \asc(\lceil\alpha\rceil,d)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:point} it suffices that $\lceil\alpha\rceil+\lfloor\beta\rfloor<2d$; and
$\lceil\alpha\rceil < \alpha+1$, $\lfloor\beta\rfloor \le \beta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deployment theorem]\label{thm:deploy}
Let $N = pq$ with $p,q>0$ real, $p$ an integer, and $r = q/p$.  If $1 \le 2m(r)\sqrt N$, then
\[
  \Bigl\lceil \sqrt{N/2}\,\Bigr\rceil + \Bigl\lfloor \sqrt N \Bigr\rfloor \;<\; 2p,
\]
i.e.\ on the integer window the sqrt-descending scan strictly beats window-ascending.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $p = \sqrt N/\sqrt r$, we have $r^{-1/2}\sqrt N = p$ and hence
$2m(r)\sqrt N = 2p - \sqrt N - \sqrt{N/2}$.  The hypothesis therefore reads
$\sqrt{N/2}+\sqrt N+1 \le 2p$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:halfstep} with $\alpha = \sqrt{N/2}$,
$\beta = \sqrt N$, $d = p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Explicit threshold]\label{cor:threshold}
If $r < r^\star$ then $m(r)>0$ and every key with $\sqrt N \ge 1/(2m(r))$ is won by
sqrt-descending.  For deployed-style ratios the threshold is a small constant: at $r = 5/4$,
$m(5/4) = 0.04044\ldots$, so $N \ge 154$ suffices.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Per-key aggregation]\label{thm:agg}
Let $S$ be a nonempty finite pool, each key $i$ with its own integer window $[a_i,b_i]$ and
divisor $d_i$.  If $a_i+b_i<2d_i$ for all $i$, then
$\sum_i \dsc(b_i,d_i) < \sum_i \asc(a_i,d_i)$.  If instead $a_i+b_i \le 2d_i$ for all $i$ with
strict inequality for at least one index, the same conclusion holds.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:point} gives the inequality termwise; summing over a nonempty index set with at
least one strict term preserves strictness.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Weighted-tilt law]\label{thm:weighted}
Let a pool of $n$ keys have windows $[a_i,b_i]$, lengths $L_i = b_i-a_i>0$ and tilts
$z_i = (d_i-a_i)/L_i$.  Put $\bar L = n^{-1}\sum_i L_i$ and
$z_w = \bigl(\sum_i L_i z_i\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_i L_i\bigr)$.  Then
\[
  \frac{T_{\dsc}}{T_{\asc}} = \frac{\bar L(1-z_w)+1}{\bar L\,z_w+1},
\]
and descending wins the pool total if and only if $z_w > 1/2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$T_{\asc} = \sum_i(d_i-a_i+1) = \sum_i L_i z_i + n = n(\bar L z_w+1)$, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cons} $T_{\dsc} = \sum_i(L_i+2) - T_{\asc} = n(\bar L(1-z_w)+1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Direction of the weighting bias]\label{rem:bias}
The weight $L_i$ is proportional to $\sqrt{N_i}$, and at fixed small factor a larger ratio means
a larger $N$ and a longer window.  Since the tilt decreases in the ratio
(Proposition~\ref{prop:mono}), long-window keys are systematically low-tilt keys, so
$z_w \le \bar z$ whenever the pool has a spread of ratios: the weighting biases the measured
speedup \emph{in favour of the ascending scan}.  The bias grows with the ratio spread and
vanishes as the pool concentrates on a single ratio.
\end{remark}

\section{Comparison with measurement}\label{sec:measure}

A simulation study generated four pools of $n = 600$ semiprimes each at bit length $b = 15$ with
a fixed seed, using exact-uniform sieve-index prime sampling, touch counts computed directly
from the scan definitions, and bootstrap standard errors from eight batches.  Reported values
($S>1$ means window-ascending wins):

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llccc@{}}
\toprule
Pool & Window & Measured $\bar z$ (95\% CI) & Measured $S \pm$ SE & In-window \\
\midrule
Hard-balance control    & canonical & $0.4114$ $[0.3887,0.4341]$ & $1.5896 \pm 0.0538$ & $1.000$ \\
Independent same-bitlen & canonical & $0.6356$ $[0.6150,0.6562]$ & $0.5578 \pm 0.0217$ & $1.000$ \\
Narrow high-ratio       & $R=4.5$   & $0.0558$ $[0.0530,0.0586]$ & $17.345 \pm 0.4654$ & $0$ \\
Wide ratio band         & $R=8.0$   & $0.5979$ $[0.5765,0.6194]$ & $0.5505 \pm 0.0230$ & $0.582$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Control pool.}  Theorem~\ref{thm:unif} gives $\bar z = \sqrt2-1 = 0.41421$,
        inside $[0.3887,0.4341]$.  The measured speedup $1.5896$ exceeds the unweighted
        tilt-only value $\sqrt2 = 1.41421$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:weighted} explains the gap
        exactly: this pool spreads its ratio over the whole band, so by Remark~\ref{rem:bias}
        the window-length-weighted mean tilt falls below the unweighted one.  An independent
        reconstruction of a $600$-key, $15$-bit ratio-uniform pool gives $\bar z = 0.4107$
        (matching the reported $0.4114$) but $z_w = 0.3856$, whence $(1-z_w)/z_w = 1.593$,
        reproducing the reported $1.5896$ within its standard error.
  \item \textbf{Deployed pool.}  Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives $\bar z = 0.642977$, inside
        $[0.6150,0.6562]$; Corollary~\ref{cor:loss} gives $S = 0.555265$, inside
        $0.5578 \pm 0.0217$.  Both are predictions, not fits.  Here the weighting bias is
        small, because the density $4/r^2-1$ is concentrated: a $600$-key reconstruction gives
        $\bar z = 0.6537$ against $z_w = 0.6583$, a shift below $0.005$, in the direction that
        makes ascending look \emph{worse}.
  \item \textbf{In-window fractions.}  Corollary~\ref{cor:bitlen} explains the $1.000$ values
        for the canonical-window pools: equal bit length forces balance.  The ascending scan was
        well defined on every deployed-style key and still lost.
  \item \textbf{Wide-band pool.}  Measured in the canonical window on a pool only $58\%$ of
        which lies inside it, so not directly comparable to $1/(1+\sqrt8)$; the sign, however,
        agrees.
  \item \textbf{Narrow high-ratio pool.}  The $17\times$ figure is a pinning artefact requiring
        advance knowledge of the declared ratio support --- information invisible from $N$ ---
        and is an illustration of Theorem~\ref{thm:tieR}, not an attack.
\end{itemize}

Agreement between the closed form $\sqrt2-1$, the analytic control target, and independent
replication of the control at a different bit length establishes that the measurement machinery
is sound; the deployed-pool reversal is therefore a property of the population, not of the
harness.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Scan-order oracle.}  Given a generator as a ratio law $\mu$ on $[1,R]$, compute
$\bar z = \int z_R\,d\mu$; output ``descending'' if $\bar z>1/2$, ``ascending'' if $\bar z<1/2$,
with predicted speedup $(L(1-\bar z)+1)/(L\bar z+1)$.  Cost: one integral; closed forms
$1/(1+\sqrt R)$ and $(9-5\sqrt2)/3$ for the two solved classes.

\paragraph{Per-key margin test.}  Given $N$ and a hypothesised ratio $r$, compute $m(r)$; if
$m(r)>0$ and $\sqrt N \ge 1/(2m(r))$, Theorem~\ref{thm:deploy} certifies that descending wins on
that key.  Cost: $O(1)$.

\paragraph{Empirical tilt estimation.}  For a pool of factored semiprimes, compute each integer
window and tilt and average; read the pool speedup from Theorem~\ref{thm:speedup}.  Cost:
$O(n)$ square roots.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What is established}

The scan-order contest is completely solved at the level of populations:
\[
  \bar z_{\text{ratio-uniform}} = \sqrt2-1 = 0.41421\ldots \;<\; \tfrac12 \;<\;
  \tfrac{9-5\sqrt2}{3} = 0.64298\ldots = \bar z_{\text{independent}} .
\]
The tie ratio $24-16\sqrt2 \approx 1.3726$ sits strictly inside the balance band, so the natural
hypothesis ``enforce balance and the ascending scan pays'' is provably wrong; and
$1 < 4R/(1+\sqrt R)^2 < 4$ shows no window redesign repairs it.

\subsection{What is not claimed}

No factoring speedup is claimed.  Both scans are exhaustive searches of a window of length
$\Theta(\sqrt N)$ and are exponential in the bit length; a constant factor of $1.8$ either way is
of no cryptanalytic consequence.  Nor is any weakness in deployed key generation implied ---
quite the reverse: deployed generation is \emph{adversarial} to the hoped-for reordering gain,
purely as a consequence of the geometry of independent sampling.  The $17\times$ figure on the
narrow high-ratio pool is a pinning artefact, not a deployable advantage.

\subsection{Limits of transfer}

The continuum model treats primes in a bit-length window as uniform points; classical heuristics
for prime distribution make this a good approximation at scale, but the transfer was assumed
rather than established, with only small-scale exhaustive enumeration performed.  The direction
of the approximation error is favourable: additional filtering by a real generator narrows the
ratio band further toward $1$, which by Proposition~\ref{prop:mono} \emph{increases} the tilt.
The simulations were run at $15$-bit scale, where the $O(1/L)$ correction is visible; at
cryptographic sizes the exact law and the predictor are indistinguishable.

\subsection{The methodological point}

The reported advantage was a joint property of ``ascending scan'' and ``ratio-uniform sampler'',
and no amount of tuning the algorithm on that sampler could have revealed the reversal.  What
revealed it was writing the sampler as a probability law, pushing it through the cost model, and
reading off a closed form.

\section{Future directions}

\paragraph{Tilt spectrum of a general generation law.}  The contest factors through one linear
functional $\E[z(r)]$, so classifying generators reduces to classifying ratio laws by a single
moment.  Theorem~\ref{thm:theta} settles the power-law family, with crossing exponent exactly
$3/2$.  \emph{Conjecture:} for every ratio law $\mu$ on $[1,2]$, $\E_\mu[z] = 1/2$ forces $\mu$
to put mass on both sides of $r^\star$; the quantitative question --- how small can
$\mu\bigl((r^\star,2]\bigr)$ be for a tied law --- remains open.

\paragraph{Unequal-bit-length generators.}  Theorem~\ref{thm:main} used only the area of a
region inside a square; for bit lengths $b$ and $b+k$ the region becomes a rectangle
$[1,2]\times[2^{k},2^{k+1}]$, whose slice areas remain elementary.  \emph{Conjecture:} for
$k \ge 1$ the ratio never falls below $2^{k} \ge 2$, so the small factor leaves the canonical
window entirely and no admissible multiplier $R < 2^{k}$ restores it; the ascending scan becomes
undefined rather than merely worse.

\paragraph{Higher moments.}  The pool speedup depends only on the mean tilt, but the per-key win
probability (Theorem~\ref{thm:freq}) is an independent statistic.  A two-parameter description
$(\E[z], \Prb[z>1/2])$ would characterise both verdicts, and both are closed-form integrals.

\paragraph{Beyond two scan orders.}  Lemma~\ref{lem:cons} applies only to the two monotone
traversals.  Minimising expected touch count over \emph{all} traversal orders given the
generator's tilt law is a scheduling problem whose solution should visit positions in decreasing
order of tilt density; quantifying the gap to the better monotone scan would complete the
reorder-class map.

\section{Conclusion}

For balanced semiprimes the choice between scanning the canonical window upward from
$\sqrt{N/2}$ and downward from $\sqrt N$ is decided by a single scalar, the mean tilt --- and
that scalar is a property of the key generator, not of any key.  Ratio-uniform populations have
mean tilt exactly $\sqrt2-1$ and favour ascending by exactly $\sqrt2$; independent
same-bit-length populations, which is what deployed generators produce, have ratio density
$4/r^2-1$ and mean tilt exactly $(9-5\sqrt2)/3$, and favour descending, with ascending losing
about $44\%$ of the work.  The tie occurs at ratio $24-16\sqrt2 \approx 1.3726$, strictly inside
the balance band, and since the tie ratio for any multiplier $R$ lies in $(1,4)$, no window
redesign repairs the deficit.  The hoped-for reordering advantage exists, but only on
populations no deployed generator emits.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

SQRT2: float = math.sqrt(2.0)
CRITICAL_RATIO: float = 24.0 - 16.0 * SQRT2          # r* = 1.3725830...
UNIFORM_MEAN_TILT: float = SQRT2 - 1.0               # 0.4142135...
INDEPENDENT_MEAN_TILT: float = (9.0 - 5.0 * SQRT2) / 3.0   # 0.6429773...


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Scan costs, tilt, and the exact speedup law
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def asc_cost(a: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Touch count of a window-ascending scan of [a, b] stopping at divisor d."""
    return d - a + 1


def desc_cost(b: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Touch count of a sqrt-descending scan of [a, b] stopping at divisor d."""
    return b - d + 1


def tilt(a: int, b: int, d: float) -> float:
    """Normalised height of d inside the window [a, b]:  0 at bottom, 1 at top."""
    return (float(d) - a) / (b - a)


def exact_speedup(mean_tilt: float, window_length: float) -> float:
    """Exact pool speedup S = (L(1 - z) + 1) / (L z + 1) of ascending over descending."""
    return (window_length * (1.0 - mean_tilt) + 1.0) / (window_length * mean_tilt + 1.0)


def tilt_only_predictor(mean_tilt: float) -> float:
    """The L -> infinity limit of the exact speedup:  (1 - z)/z."""
    return (1.0 - mean_tilt) / mean_tilt


def predictor_error_bound(mean_tilt: float, window_length: float) -> float:
    """Rigorous bound |exact - predictor| <= 1/(L z^2)."""
    return 1.0 / (window_length * mean_tilt ** 2)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  The ratio law
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def z_of_ratio(r: float) -> float:
    """Tilt of the small factor of a semiprime of prime ratio r, canonical window."""
    return (1.0 / math.sqrt(r) - 1.0 / SQRT2) / (1.0 - 1.0 / SQRT2)


def z_of_ratio_general(window_multiplier: float, r: float) -> float:
    """Tilt law for the window (sqrt(N/R), sqrt(N)]."""
    inv = 1.0 / math.sqrt(window_multiplier)
    return (1.0 / math.sqrt(r) - inv) / (1.0 - inv)


def critical_ratio_general(window_multiplier: float) -> float:
    """Tie ratio for multiplier R:  r*(R) = 4R / (1 + sqrt(R))^2."""
    s = math.sqrt(window_multiplier)
    return 4.0 * window_multiplier / (1.0 + s) ** 2


def margin(r: float) -> float:
    """Top-heaviness margin m(r) = r^{-1/2} - (1 + 2^{-1/2})/2; positive iff r < r*."""
    return 1.0 / math.sqrt(r) - (1.0 + 1.0 / SQRT2) / 2.0


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The independent same-bit-length model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ratio_area(r: float) -> float:
    """Area of {(p, q) in [1,2]^2 : p <= q <= r p}, exactly 5/2 - 2/r - r/2."""
    return 2.5 - 2.0 / r - r / 2.0


def ratio_density(r: float) -> float:
    """Ratio density of two independent uniform draws from [1,2] given p <= q."""
    return 4.0 / r ** 2 - 1.0


def ratio_cdf(s: float) -> float:
    """P[r <= s] = 5 - 4/s - s for 1 <= s <= 2."""
    return 5.0 - 4.0 / s - s


def simpson(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, n: int = 200_000) -> float:
    """Composite Simpson quadrature on [a, b] with an even number of panels."""
    if n % 2:
        n += 1
    h = (b - a) / n
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += (4.0 if i % 2 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return total * h / 3.0


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Prime utilities (small scale, for honest end-to-end simulation)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def primes_up_to(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """Sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    if limit < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i::i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i::i]))
    return [i for i in range(limit + 1) if sieve[i]]


def primes_in_bit_window(bits: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes p with 2^(bits-1) <= p < 2^bits."""
    lo, hi = 1 << (bits - 1), 1 << bits
    return [p for p in primes_up_to(hi - 1) if p >= lo]


def integer_window(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """The true integer scan window [ceil(sqrt(N/2)), floor(sqrt(N))]."""
    a = math.ceil(math.sqrt(n / 2.0))
    b = math.isqrt(n)
    return a, b

# 5.  Pool statistics
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def pool_statistics(pairs: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> dict:
    """
    Exact touch-count statistics for a pool of (p, q) with p <= q, each key
    scanned in its own integer window.  Returns mean tilt, totals, and the
    measured speedup S = total_desc / total_asc.
    """
    tilts: List[float] = []
    total_asc = 0
    total_desc = 0
    in_window = 0
    lengths: List[int] = []
    weighted = 0.0
    for p, q in pairs:
        n = p * q
        a, b = integer_window(n)
        if not (a <= p <= b):
            continue
        in_window += 1
        lengths.append(b - a)
        z = tilt(a, b, p)
        tilts.append(z)
        weighted += (b - a) * z
        total_asc += asc_cost(a, p)
        total_desc += desc_cost(b, p)
    mean_tilt = sum(tilts) / len(tilts) if tilts else float("nan")
    return {
        "n": len(pairs),
        "in_window_fraction": in_window / len(pairs),
        "mean_tilt": mean_tilt,
        "weighted_mean_tilt": weighted / sum(lengths) if lengths else float("nan"),
        "mean_window_length": sum(lengths) / len(lengths) if lengths else float("nan"),
        "total_asc": total_asc,
        "total_desc": total_desc,
        "speedup": total_desc / total_asc if total_asc else float("nan"),
        "descending_wins": total_desc < total_asc,
    }


def independent_pool(bits: int, size: int, rng: random.Random) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Deployed style: two primes drawn independently and uniformly from one bit window."""
    ps = primes_in_bit_window(bits)
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    while len(out) < size:
        p, q = rng.choice(ps), rng.choice(ps)
        if p == q:
            continue
        out.append((min(p, q), max(p, q)))
    return out


def ratio_uniform_pool(bits: int, size: int, rng: random.Random) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """
    Hard-balance control: the prime ratio is (approximately) uniform on [1, 2].
    Draw p from the bit window and a target ratio r uniformly from [1, 2], then
    take q to be the prime nearest to r*p drawn from a table extending one bit
    beyond the window, so the realised ratio is not clamped at the window edge.
    """
    small = primes_in_bit_window(bits)
    big = [x for x in primes_up_to(1 << (bits + 1)) if x >= (1 << (bits - 1))]
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    while len(out) < size:
        p = rng.choice(small)
        r = rng.uniform(1.0, 2.0)
        target = r * p
        q = min(big, key=lambda x: abs(x - target))
        if q <= p or q >= 2 * p:
            continue
        out.append((p, q))
    return out


def exhaustive_independent_pool(bits: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Every unordered pair of distinct primes of the given bit length."""
    ps = primes_in_bit_window(bits)
    return [(ps[i], ps[j]) for i in range(len(ps)) for j in range(i + 1, len(ps))]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

SQRT2: float = math.sqrt(2.0)
CRITICAL_RATIO: float = 24.0 - 16.0 * SQRT2          # r* = 1.3725830...
UNIFORM_MEAN_TILT: float = SQRT2 - 1.0               # 0.4142135...
INDEPENDENT_MEAN_TILT: float = (9.0 - 5.0 * SQRT2) / 3.0   # 0.6429773...


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Scan costs, tilt, and the exact speedup law
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def asc_cost(a: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Touch count of a window-ascending scan of [a, b] stopping at divisor d."""
    return d - a + 1


def desc_cost(b: int, d: int) -> int:
    """Touch count of a sqrt-descending scan of [a, b] stopping at divisor d."""
    return b - d + 1


def tilt(a: int, b: int, d: float) -> float:
    """Normalised height of d inside the window [a, b]:  0 at bottom, 1 at top."""
    return (float(d) - a) / (b - a)


def exact_speedup(mean_tilt: float, window_length: float) -> float:
    """Exact pool speedup S = (L(1 - z) + 1) / (L z + 1) of ascending over descending."""
    return (window_length * (1.0 - mean_tilt) + 1.0) / (window_length * mean_tilt + 1.0)


def tilt_only_predictor(mean_tilt: float) -> float:
    """The L -> infinity limit of the exact speedup:  (1 - z)/z."""
    return (1.0 - mean_tilt) / mean_tilt


def predictor_error_bound(mean_tilt: float, window_length: float) -> float:
    """Rigorous bound |exact - predictor| <= 1/(L z^2)."""
    return 1.0 / (window_length * mean_tilt ** 2)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  The ratio law
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def z_of_ratio(r: float) -> float:
    """Tilt of the small factor of a semiprime of prime ratio r, canonical window."""
    return (1.0 / math.sqrt(r) - 1.0 / SQRT2) / (1.0 - 1.0 / SQRT2)


def z_of_ratio_general(window_multiplier: float, r: float) -> float:
    """Tilt law for the window (sqrt(N/R), sqrt(N)]."""
    inv = 1.0 / math.sqrt(window_multiplier)
    return (1.0 / math.sqrt(r) - inv) / (1.0 - inv)


def critical_ratio_general(window_multiplier: float) -> float:
    """Tie ratio for multiplier R:  r*(R) = 4R / (1 + sqrt(R))^2."""
    s = math.sqrt(window_multiplier)
    return 4.0 * window_multiplier / (1.0 + s) ** 2


def margin(r: float) -> float:
    """Top-heaviness margin m(r) = r^{-1/2} - (1 + 2^{-1/2})/2; positive iff r < r*."""
    return 1.0 / math.sqrt(r) - (1.0 + 1.0 / SQRT2) / 2.0


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The independent same-bit-length model
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ratio_area(r: float) -> float:
    """Area of {(p, q) in [1,2]^2 : p <= q <= r p}, exactly 5/2 - 2/r - r/2."""
    return 2.5 - 2.0 / r - r / 2.0


def ratio_density(r: float) -> float:
    """Ratio density of two independent uniform draws from [1,2] given p <= q."""
    return 4.0 / r ** 2 - 1.0


def ratio_cdf(s: float) -> float:
    """P[r <= s] = 5 - 4/s - s for 1 <= s <= 2."""
    return 5.0 - 4.0 / s - s


def simpson(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, n: int = 200_000) -> float:
    """Composite Simpson quadrature on [a, b] with an even number of panels."""
    if n % 2:
        n += 1
    h = (b - a) / n
    total = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += (4.0 if i % 2 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return total * h / 3.0


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Prime utilities (small scale, for honest end-to-end simulation)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def primes_up_to(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    """Sieve of Eratosthenes."""
    if limit < 2:
        return []
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(limit ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i::i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i::i]))
    return [i for i in range(limit + 1) if sieve[i]]


def primes_in_bit_window(bits: int) -> List[int]:
    """All primes p with 2^(bits-1) <= p < 2^bits."""
    lo, hi = 1 << (bits - 1), 1 << bits
    return [p for p in primes_up_to(hi - 1) if p >= lo]


def integer_window(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """The true integer scan window [ceil(sqrt(N/2)), floor(sqrt(N))]."""
    a = math.ceil(math.sqrt(n / 2.0))
    b = math.isqrt(n)
    return a, b


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Pool statistics
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def pool_statistics(pairs: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> dict:
    """
    Exact touch-count statistics for a pool of (p, q) with p <= q, each key
    scanned in its own integer window.  Returns mean tilt, totals, and the
    measured speedup S = total_desc / total_asc.
    """
    tilts: List[float] = []
    total_asc = 0
    total_desc = 0
    in_window = 0
    lengths: List[int] = []
    weighted = 0.0
    for p, q in pairs:
        n = p * q
        a, b = integer_window(n)
        if not (a <= p <= b):
            continue
        in_window += 1
        lengths.append(b - a)
        z = tilt(a, b, p)
        tilts.append(z)
        weighted += (b - a) * z
        total_asc += asc_cost(a, p)
        total_desc += desc_cost(b, p)
    mean_tilt = sum(tilts) / len(tilts) if tilts else float("nan")
    return {
        "n": len(pairs),
        "in_window_fraction": in_window / len(pairs),
        "mean_tilt": mean_tilt,
        "weighted_mean_tilt": weighted / sum(lengths) if lengths else float("nan"),
        "mean_window_length": sum(lengths) / len(lengths) if lengths else float("nan"),
        "total_asc": total_asc,
        "total_desc": total_desc,
        "speedup": total_desc / total_asc if total_asc else float("nan"),
        "descending_wins": total_desc < total_asc,
    }


def independent_pool(bits: int, size: int, rng: random.Random) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Deployed style: two primes drawn independently and uniformly from one bit window."""
    ps = primes_in_bit_window(bits)
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    while len(out) < size:
        p, q = rng.choice(ps), rng.choice(ps)
        if p == q:
            continue
        out.append((min(p, q), max(p, q)))
    return out


def ratio_uniform_pool(bits: int, size: int, rng: random.Random) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """
    Hard-balance control: the prime ratio is (approximately) uniform on [1, 2].
    Draw p from the bit window and a target ratio r uniformly from [1, 2], then
    take q to be the prime nearest to r*p drawn from a table extending one bit
    beyond the window, so the realised ratio is not clamped at the window edge.
    """
    small = primes_in_bit_window(bits)
    big = [x for x in primes_up_to(1 << (bits + 1)) if x >= (1 << (bits - 1))]
    out: List[Tuple[int, int]] = []
    while len(out) < size:
        p = rng.choice(small)
        r = rng.uniform(1.0, 2.0)
        target = r * p
        q = min(big, key=lambda x: abs(x - target))
        if q <= p or q >= 2 * p:
            continue
        out.append((p, q))
    return out


def exhaustive_independent_pool(bits: int) -> List[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Every unordered pair of distinct primes of the given bit length."""
    ps = primes_in_bit_window(bits)
    return [(ps[i], ps[j]) for i in range(len(ps)) for j in range(i + 1, len(ps))]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

SQRT2 = math.sqrt(2.0)
R_STAR = 24.0 - 16.0 * SQRT2
TOL = 1e-9

_failures = 0


def check(name: str, got: float, want: float, tol: float = TOL) -> None:
    global _failures
    ok = abs(got - want) <= tol * max(1.0, abs(want))
    if not ok:
        _failures += 1
    print(f"  [{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}]  {name:<52} got {got:.12f}  want {want:.12f}"
          f"  |diff| {abs(got - want):.2e}")


def simpson(f: Callable[[float], float], a: float, b: float, n: int = 400_000) -> float:
    if n % 2:
        n += 1
    h = (b - a) / n
    s = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        s += (4.0 if i % 2 else 2.0) * f(a + i * h)
    return s * h / 3.0


def z_of_ratio(r: float, R: float = 2.0) -> float:
    inv = 1.0 / math.sqrt(R)
    return (1.0 / math.sqrt(r) - inv) / (1.0 - inv)


def ratio_area(r: float) -> float:
    return 2.5 - 2.0 / r - r / 2.0


def ratio_density(r: float) -> float:
    return 4.0 / r ** 2 - 1.0


def tie_ratio(R: float) -> float:
    s = math.sqrt(R)
    return 4.0 * R / (1.0 + s) ** 2


def primes_in_bit_window(bits: int) -> List[int]:
    hi = 1 << bits
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * hi
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(hi ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i::i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i::i]))
    return [i for i in range(1 << (bits - 1), hi) if sieve[i]]


def exhaustive(bits: int) -> Tuple[float, float, int]:
    """Mean tilt and exact touch-count speedup over ALL same-bit-length prime pairs."""
    ps = primes_in_bit_window(bits)
    tilts: List[float] = []
    total_asc = total_desc = 0
    for i in range(len(ps)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(ps)):
            p, q = ps[i], ps[j]
            n = p * q
            a = math.ceil(math.sqrt(n / 2.0))
            b = math.isqrt(n)
            if b <= a or not (a <= p <= b):
                continue
            tilts.append((p - a) / (b - a))
            total_asc += p - a + 1
            total_desc += b - p + 1
    return sum(tilts) / len(tilts), total_desc / total_asc, len(tilts)

def integer_window(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Exact [ceil(sqrt(N/2)), floor(sqrt(N))] using integer square roots only."""
    a = math.isqrt((n + 1) // 2)
    while 2 * a * a < n:
        a += 1
    while a > 1 and 2 * (a - 1) * (a - 1) >= n:
        a -= 1
    return a, math.isqrt(n)

    i.e. when the pair is not balanced -- there the ascending scan is undefined.

    tilts: List[float] = []
    lengths: List[int] = []
    weighted = 0.0
    total_asc = total_desc = 0
    for p, q in pairs:

        n = p * q
        a, b = integer_window(n)
        if b <= a or not (a <= p <= b):

        L = b - a
        z = (p - a) / L
        tilts.append(z)
        lengths.append(L)
        weighted += L * z
        total_asc += p - a + 1
        total_desc += b - p + 1
    if not tilts:

        in_window=len(tilts),
        mean_window_length=sum(lengths) / len(lengths),
        mean_tilt=sum(tilts) / len(tilts),
        weighted_mean_tilt=weighted / sum(lengths),
        total_ascending=total_asc,
        total_descending=total_desc,

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

SQRT2 = math.sqrt(2.0)
R_STAR = 24.0 - 16.0 * SQRT2
Z_INDEPENDENT = (9.0 - 5.0 * SQRT2) / 3.0


def critical_ratio_general(R: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    s = np.sqrt(R)
    return 4.0 * R / (1.0 + s) ** 2


def z_of_ratio(r: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    return (1.0 / np.sqrt(r) - 1.0 / SQRT2) / (1.0 - 1.0 / SQRT2)


def primes_in_bit_window(bits: int) -> List[int]:
    hi = 1 << bits
    sieve = bytearray([1]) * hi
    sieve[0] = sieve[1] = 0
    for i in range(2, int(hi ** 0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            sieve[i * i::i] = bytearray(len(sieve[i * i::i]))
    return [i for i in range(1 << (bits - 1), hi) if sieve[i]]


def exhaustive_tilts(bits: int) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    ps = primes_in_bit_window(bits)
    ratios, tilts = [], []
    for i in range(len(ps)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(ps)):
            p, q = ps[i], ps[j]
            n = p * q
            a = math.ceil(math.sqrt(n / 2.0))
            b = math.isqrt(n)
            if not (a <= p <= b) or b <= a:
                continue
            ratios.append(q / p)
            tilts.append((p - a) / (b - a))
    return np.array(ratios), np.array(tilts)

    ax.set_xlim(1.0, 60.0)
    ax.set_ylim(0.8, 4.4)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"window multiplier $R$")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"tie ratio $r^\star(R)$")
    ax.set_title("A.  No window pushes the tie past $4$", fontsize=12.5)
    ax.legend(fontsize=9.5, loc="lower right")

    # ---- Panel B: ratio-uniform mean tilt for every window --------------
    ax = axes[1]
    ax.plot(R, 1.0 / (1.0 + np.sqrt(R)), color="#123a6b", lw=2.6,
            label=r"ratio-uniform mean tilt $1/(1+\sqrt{R})$")
    ax.axhline(0.5, color="#555555", ls="--", lw=1.4, label=r"threshold $1/2$")
    ax.axhline(Z_INDEPENDENT, color="#8b0000", lw=2.2,

    ax.fill_between(R, 0, 0.5, color="#c8dcf6", alpha=0.5)

    ax.set_xlim(1.0, 60.0)
    ax.set_ylim(0.0, 0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"window multiplier $R$")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"mean tilt $\bar z$")
    ax.set_title("B.  Ratio-spread pools are bottom-heavy for every $R$", fontsize=12.5)
    ax.legend(fontsize=9.5, loc="upper right")

    ratios, tilts = exhaustive_tilts(10)

    ax.set_ylim(0.0, 1.0)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"prime ratio $r=q/p$")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"realised tilt in the integer window")
    ax.set_title("C.  Real primes land on the exact curve", fontsize=12.5)
    ax.legend(fontsize=9.5, loc="upper right")

    fig.suptitle("Window design cannot rescue the ascending scan", fontsize=15, y=1.02)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("window_nogo.png", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight")
    print("wrote window_nogo.png  (empirical mean tilt %.6f vs exact %.6f)"
          % (tilts.mean(), Z_INDEPENDENT))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

<script>
"use strict";
const SQRT2 = Math.SQRT2;
const el = id => document.getElementById(id);

/* ---------------- mathematics ---------------- */
function zOfRatio(R, r) {
  const inv = 1 / Math.sqrt(R);
  return (1 / Math.sqrt(r) - inv) / (1 - inv);
}
function tieRatio(R) {
  const s = Math.sqrt(R);
  return 4 * R / ((1 + s) * (1 + s));
}
function exactSpeedup(z, L) {
  return (L * (1 - z) + 1) / (L * z + 1);
}
/* exact closed forms proved for the two solved generator classes */
const Z_UNIFORM_CANON     = SQRT2 - 1;                 /* ratio-uniform on [1,2]     */
const Z_INDEPENDENT       = (9 - 5 * SQRT2) / 3;       /* independent same bit length */
const P_INDEPENDENT       = (5 * SQRT2 - 6) / (9 - 5 * SQRT2);
const R_STAR_CANON        = 24 - 16 * SQRT2;

/* ---------------- sampling ---------------- */
function sampleRatios(law, R, theta, r0, n) {
  const out = new Float64Array(n);
  if (law === "indep") {
    /* two independent uniforms on [1,2], conditioned on p <= q: density 4/r^2 - 1 */
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      const p = 1 + Math.random(), q = 1 + Math.random();
      out[i] = Math.max(p, q) / Math.min(p, q);
    }
  } else if (law === "unif") {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) out[i] = 1 + Math.random() * (R - 1);
  } else if (law === "power") {
    /* density proportional to r^-theta on [1,2] by rejection against its maximum */
    const fmax = theta >= 0 ? 1 : Math.pow(2, -theta);
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      for (;;) {
        const r = 1 + Math.random();
        if (Math.random() * fmax <= Math.pow(r, -theta)) { out[i] = r; break; }
      }
    }
  } else {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) out[i] = r0;
  }
  return out;
}

/* ---------------- state ---------------- */
let ratios = null;

function currentParams() {
  return {
    law: el("law").value,
    R: parseFloat(el("R").value),
    theta: parseFloat(el("theta").value),
    r0: parseFloat(el("r0").value),
    n: parseInt(el("n").value, 10),
    L: parseInt(el("L").value, 10)
  };
}

function resample() {
  const p = currentParams();
  ratios = sampleRatios(p.law, p.R, p.theta, p.r0, p.n);
}

/* ---------------- analysis ---------------- */
function analyse() {
  const p = currentParams();
  const tilts = [];
  let below = 0;
  const rs = tieRatio(p.R);
  for (let i = 0; i < ratios.length; i++) {
    const r = ratios[i];
    if (r > p.R) continue;            /* factor outside the window: scan undefined */
    const z = zOfRatio(p.R, r);
    tilts.push(z);
    if (r < rs) below++;
  }
  const inwin = tilts.length / ratios.length;
  let s = 0;
  for (const z of tilts) s += z;
  const zbar = tilts.length ? s / tilts.length : NaN;
  return { p, tilts, zbar, inwin, fracDesc: tilts.length ? below / tilts.length : NaN, rs };
}

/* ---------------- rendering ---------------- */
function fitCanvas(c) {
  const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
  const w = c.clientWidth;
  c.width = w * dpr;
  c.height = parseInt(c.getAttribute("height"), 10) * dpr;
  const ctx = c.getContext("2d");
  ctx.setTransform(dpr, 0, 0, dpr, 0, 0);
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, w, c.height / dpr);
  return { ctx, w, h: c.height / dpr };
}

function drawWindow(a) {
  const { ctx, w, h } = fitCanvas(el("windowCanvas"));
  const padL = 46, padR = 22, top = 26, barY = 96, barH = 34;
  const W = w - padL - padR;

  ctx.font = "12px ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif";
  ctx.fillStyle = "#6b6257";
  ctx.fillText("bottom of window  √(N/R)", padL, top - 8);
  ctx.textAlign = "right";
  ctx.fillText("√N  top of window", padL + W, top - 8);
  ctx.textAlign = "left";

  /* the window strip */
  const grad = ctx.createLinearGradient(padL, 0, padL + W, 0);
  grad.addColorStop(0, "#eef3fb");
  grad.addColorStop(1, "#fdeeee");

  "interactive_layout": "# Which way should you walk? A guided tour of generator tilt

> **The question in one sentence.** A large number $N$ is the product of two primes of similar size. You are going to search for the smaller one by walking across a narrow window of candidates. Should you walk *up* the window, or *down* from $\sqrt N$? The answer is not a coin flip — and it is decided by something you might not expect: the habits of the machine that made the key.

By the end of this page you will have derived, checked, and *played with* four exact numbers:

| | |
|---|---|
| $24 - 16\sqrt2 = 1.372583\ldots$ | the prime ratio at which the two walks cost exactly the same |
| $\sqrt2 - 1 = 0.414214\ldots$ | the mean position of the factor for a laboratory population |
| $(9 - 5\sqrt2)/3 = 0.642977\ldots$ | the mean position for a *realistic* population |
| $\theta^\star = 3/2$ | the exact boundary of the whole one-parameter family in between |

The first two say "walk up." The third says "walk down." That reversal is the story.

---

## 1. The window, and why there is a choice at all

Let $N = pq$ with $p \le q$. You never need to look above $\sqrt N$. And if the two primes are **balanced** — meaning $q < 2p$, neither more than twice the other — then $p^2 \le N < 2p^2$, which pins the small factor into

$$p \in \left(\sqrt{N/2},\ \sqrt{N}\right],$$

a strip of length about $0.293\sqrt N$. Call it the **canonical window**.

<details>
<summary><strong>Why balance is exactly window membership</strong> (click to expand)</summary>

For positive integers, cancel the factor $p$:

- $p^2 \le pq$ if and only if $p \le q$;
- $pq < 2p^2 = p \cdot 2p$ if and only if $q < 2p$.

So "the small factor lies in the canonical window" and "the pair is balanced" are the *same statement*. A useful corollary: if $p$ and $q$ have the same bit length, say $2^{b-1} \le p \le q < 2^b$, then $q < 2^b = 2\cdot 2^{b-1} \le 2p$ automatically. **Same bit length forces balance**, so every key produced by the standard recipe lands inside its window and the upward scan is always well defined on it. Keep this in mind: it means the upward scan's later defeat cannot be blamed on missing keys.

</details>

Inside the window you may walk **up** from the bottom, costing $d - a + 1$ touches to reach the divisor $d$ in a window $[a,b]$, or **down** from the top, costing $b - d + 1$.

---

## 2. One scalar decides everything

Add the two costs:

$$(d - a + 1) + (b - d + 1) = (b - a) + 2.$$

The divisor cancels. The two walks **share a fixed budget** — whatever one saves the other spends. So the entire contest reduces to *where in the window the divisor sits*. Define the **tilt**

$$z = \frac{d - a}{b - a} \in [0, 1],$$

zero at the bottom, one at the top. Walking up costs $Lz + 1$ where $L = b-a$; walking down costs $L(1-z)+1$. Averaging over a pool of keys with mean tilt $\bar z$:

$$S \;=\; \frac{\text{total downward cost}}{\text{total upward cost}} \;=\; \frac{L(1-\bar z)+1}{L\bar z+1},$$

so **descending wins if and only if $\bar z > 1/2$.** That is the whole decision rule.

<details>
<summary><strong>The large-window predictor, and exactly how wrong it is</strong></summary>

For long windows the law simplifies to the *tilt-only predictor* $(1-\bar z)/\bar z$, and the error is not merely small — it has a closed form:

$$\frac{L(1-z)+1}{Lz+1} - \frac{1-z}{z} = \frac{2z-1}{z\,(Lz+1)}.$$

Two consequences. The error **vanishes identically at $z = 1/2$**, so the predictor never gets the *winner* wrong, only the margin. And $|{\cdot}| \le 1/(Lz^2)$, which for cryptographic sizes (where $L \sim \sqrt N$) is astronomically small.

There is one genuine subtlety when keys have *different* windows: the governing average is then the one **weighted by window length**,
$$z_w = \frac{\sum_i L_i z_i}{\sum_i L_i}, \qquad S = \frac{\bar L(1-z_w)+1}{\bar L z_w + 1},$$
which is again exact. Because a larger ratio means a larger $N$ (longer window) *and* a lower tilt, this weighting drags the effective tilt down on ratio-spread pools — the reason laboratory measurements come out a little more favourable to ascending than the plain average predicts.

</details>

---

## 3. The tilt belongs to the generator, not to the key

Here is the pivot. For real $p, q > 0$ with ratio $r = q/p$, write $p = u^2$ and $q = v^2$; then $\sqrt{pq} = uv$, $\sqrt{pq/2} = uv/\sqrt2$, and dividing through by $uv$:

$$\frac{p - \sqrt{pq/2}}{\sqrt{pq} - \sqrt{pq/2}} \;=\; \frac{u/v - 2^{-1/2}}{1 - 2^{-1/2}} \;=\; z(r), \qquad z(r) = \frac{r^{-1/2} - 2^{-1/2}}{1 - 2^{-1/2}}.$$

The *size of $N$ has cancelled*. A 20-bit key and a 2048-bit key with the same ratio have the same tilt. The map $z$ is strictly decreasing with $z(1) = 1$ and $z(2) = 0$: **perfectly balanced keys sit at the top of the window**, precisely where the downward walk starts.

Setting $z(r) = 1/2$ gives the tie:

$$r^\star = 24 - 16\sqrt2 = 1.372583\ldots$$

which lies **strictly inside** the balance band $(1,2)$. Enforcing $q < 2p$ — the very condition that makes the upward scan legal — settles nothing about whether it pays.

{{visualization:0}}

---

## 4. Play with it

Now make the ideas move. Below, choose a key generator and watch its verdict form: the window fills with keys at their true tilts, the mean tilt slides across the midpoint, and the two cost bars re-race. Start with the deployed generator (the default), then switch to the ratio-uniform laboratory control and see the verdict flip.

Three experiments worth running:

1. **The reversal.** Deployed vs. ratio-uniform at $R = 2$: mean tilt $0.6430$ versus $0.4142$, on opposite sides of the midpoint.
2. **The no-go.** Keep the ratio-uniform law and drag the window multiplier $R$ from $1.05$ to $8$. The mean tilt is always below $\tfrac12$ — that is where the ascending advantage lives, and it is a laboratory artefact. Now switch to a fixed ratio just above $1$ and sweep $R$ again: the verdict never flips.
3. **The crossing.** Choose the power-law family and sweep $\theta$. Watch the mean tilt cross $\tfrac12$ at exactly $\theta = 1.5$.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

---

## 5. What a real generator actually does — solved exactly

A deployed generator does not sample a ratio. It samples two primes **independently and uniformly** from the same bit-length window and takes whatever ratio comes out. Normalise the window to $[1,2]$: what is the law of $r$?

Slice the square. The region $\{(p,q) \in [1,2]^2 : p \le q \le rp\}$ has vertical extent $\min(rp,2) - p$ above each $p$, and the formula changes at $p = 2/r$. Splitting there and integrating gives the exact area

$$A(r) = \frac52 - \frac2r - \frac r2,$$

with $A(1) = 0$ and $A(2) = 1/2$ (the half-square $p \le q$) as sanity checks. Differentiating and dividing by the total mass $1/2$ gives the **ratio density**

$$f(r) = \frac{4}{r^2} - 1 \quad \text{on } [1,2], \qquad \int_1^2 f = 1.$$

It is *not* flat: $f(1) = 3$, $f(2) = 0$. Independent same-size primes come out **nearly equal**, with median ratio about $1.219$.

<details>
<summary><strong>The main computation: integrating tilt against this density</strong></summary>

With $c = 2^{-1/2}$,

$$z(r) f(r) = \frac{1}{1-c}\left(4r^{-5/2} - r^{-1/2} - 4c\,r^{-2} + c\right),$$

each term an elementary power. An antiderivative of the bracket is

$$G(r) = -\tfrac83 r^{-3/2} - 2r^{1/2} + 4c\,r^{-1} + c\,r,$$

and $G(2) - G(1) = \tfrac{14}{3} - \tfrac{19\sqrt2}{6} = \tfrac{9-5\sqrt2}{3}(1-c)$. Dividing by $1-c$:

$$\boxed{\ \bar z_{\text{independent}} = \frac{9 - 5\sqrt2}{3} = 0.642977\ldots\ }$$

Greater than one half. The deployed generator class is **top-heavy as a theorem**, and the upward scan's exact loss is
$$\frac{1-\bar z}{\bar z} = \frac{5\sqrt2 - 6}{9 - 5\sqrt2} = 0.555265\ldots,$$
i.e. it performs about $1.80$ times the work. Moreover the reversal is typical rather than a tail effect: the probability that an individual key beats the upward scan is $5 - 4/r^\star - r^\star \approx 0.7132$, about $71\%$ of keys.

</details>

Run the exact audit yourself — it checks every closed form against quadrature *and* against exhaustive enumeration of every same-bit-length prime pair up to 12 bits:

{{demo:1}}

---

## 6. Can a different window save the upward scan? No.

The window multiplier is free: scan $(\sqrt{N/R},\,\sqrt N]$ for any $R > 1$ that the generator's balance guarantee permits. The tie ratio becomes

$$r^\star(R) = \frac{4R}{(1+\sqrt R)^2},$$

and writing $s = \sqrt R > 1$ makes the two decisive bounds one line each: $r^\star > 1 \iff 2s > 1 + s$, and $r^\star < 4 \iff s^2 < (1+s)^2$. So for **every** window there is an interval of near-balanced ratios on which ascending loses, and the tie point can never be pushed past ratio $4$. Meanwhile ratio-uniform pools on $[1,R]$ have mean tilt exactly $1/(1+\sqrt R) < \tfrac12$ for every $R$ — bottom-heaviness belongs to ratio-*spread* populations, not to any window choice.

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 7. Where exactly is the boundary? An exact rational answer

Interpolate between the two solved cases with the family whose density is proportional to $r^{-\theta}$ on $[1,2]$: $\theta = 0$ is the flat control, and larger $\theta$ piles mass against perfect balance. Writing $I(s) = \int_1^2 r^{-s}dr$, the mean tilt is $\bigl(I(\theta+\tfrac12)/I(\theta) - c\bigr)/(1-c)$, so the tie condition is $I(\theta+\tfrac12)/I(\theta) = (1+c)/2$.

<details>
<summary><strong>Two lines to $\theta^\star = 3/2$</strong></summary>

At $\theta = 3/2$: $I(2) = 1/2$ and $I(3/2) = 2 - \sqrt2$, so

$$\frac{I(2)}{I(3/2)} = \frac{1}{2(2-\sqrt2)} = \frac{2+\sqrt2}{4} = \frac{1 + 2^{-1/2}}{2},$$

using $(2-\sqrt2)(2+\sqrt2) = 2$. That is exactly the tie condition. Uniqueness follows from monotonicity: for $\theta_1 < \theta_2$ the density ratio $r^{-(\theta_2-\theta_1)}$ is decreasing, so $\mu_{\theta_2}$ is stochastically smaller, and since $z$ is strictly decreasing the mean tilt strictly increases with $\theta$.

</details>

$$\boxed{\ \theta^\star = \tfrac32\ }$$

A generator is adversarial to the upward scan exactly when its ratio density is **steeper than $r^{-3/2}$** near balance. Real independent sampling, with density behaving like $4/r^2 - 1$, comfortably is. Sweep $\theta$ in the widget above and watch the crossing land on the nose.

---

## 8. From the continuum to actual integers

A real scan runs over $[\lceil\sqrt{N/2}\rceil, \lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor]$, so rounding can eat at most a half step at each end. Define the **margin**

$$m(r) = r^{-1/2} - \tfrac12\left(1 + 2^{-1/2}\right),$$

positive exactly when $r < r^\star$. Then whenever $\sqrt N \ge 1/(2m(r))$ one has $\lceil\sqrt{N/2}\rceil + \lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor < 2p$: the downward scan strictly wins **on the true integer window**. For deployed-style ratios the threshold is tiny — at $r = 5/4$ it is $N \ge 154$ — so every key of cryptographic size clears it by an absurd margin.

## 10. What this does and does not mean

**It does mean:** the direction of a divisor scan is decided by one scalar; that scalar is a property of the key generator, not of any key; the two natural generator classes have exactly opposite verdicts; and no window redesign changes the second one.

**It does not mean any factoring speedup.** Both scans are exhaustive searches of a window of length $\Theta(\sqrt N)$ and are hopeless at cryptographic sizes; turning a $0.55$ into a $1.8$ rearranges a constant factor inside an intractable search. Nor is any weakness in key generation implied — quite the opposite: independent sampling happens to be adversarial to the hoped-for reordering gain, for free, as a consequence of geometry.

The transferable lesson is methodological. When you benchmark an algorithm on a synthetic population you are measuring *two* things, and the sampler is usually the one you thought about least. Here the entanglement was tight enough that the advantage had the **opposite sign** on synthetic and realistic inputs. What untangled it was not more benchmarking; it was writing the sampler as a probability law, pushing it through the cost model, and reading off a closed form.

Two closed forms, in fact: $\sqrt2 - 1$ for the laboratory and $(9-5\sqrt2)/3$ for the world. They sit on opposite sides of one half, and everything else follows.

/-! ## The two scan costs inside a window -/

/-- Touch count of a window-ascending scan of `[a, b]` that stops at divisor `d`. -/
def ascCost (a d : ℤ) : ℤ := d - a + 1

/-- Touch count of a sqrt-descending scan of `[a, b]` that stops at divisor `d`. -/
def descCost (b d : ℤ) : ℤ := b - d + 1

/-- **Conservation law**: the two scan orders share the window budget; their touch counts
always sum to the window length plus two. -/
theorem ascCost_add_descCost (a b d : ℤ) : ascCost a d + descCost b d = (b - a) + 2 := by
  unfold ascCost descCost; ring

theorem ascCost_pos {a d : ℤ} (h : a ≤ d) : 0 < ascCost a d := by
  unfold ascCost; omega

theorem descCost_pos {b d : ℤ} (h : d ≤ b) : 0 < descCost b d := by
  unfold descCost; omega

/-- Pointwise inversion: descending beats ascending exactly above the window midpoint. -/
theorem descCost_lt_ascCost_iff (a b d : ℤ) :
    descCost b d < ascCost a d ↔ a + b < 2 * d := by
  unfold ascCost descCost; omega

/-! ## The canonical window is the balance window -/

/-- **Window membership is exactly balance.**  For a factorisation `N = p * q` with `0 < p`,
the small factor lies in the canonical window `(√(N/2), √N]` — i.e. `p^2 ≤ N < 2p^2` —
if and only if `p ≤ q` and `q < 2p`.  In particular a generator that does *not* enforce
`q < 2p` produces keys for which window-ascending is not even well defined. -/
theorem window_iff_balanced {p q : ℕ} (hp : 0 < p) :
    (p * p ≤ p * q ∧ p * q < 2 * (p * p)) ↔ (p ≤ q ∧ q < 2 * p) := by
  have h2 : 2 * (p * p) = p * (2 * p) := by ring
  rw [h2, Nat.mul_le_mul_left_iff hp, Nat.mul_lt_mul_left hp]

/-- Enforced balance puts every key inside the window (`in_win = 1`). -/
theorem balanced_in_window {p q : ℕ} (hp : 0 < p) (h1 : p ≤ q) (h2 : q < 2 * p) :
    p * p ≤ p * q ∧ p * q < 2 * (p * p) := (window_iff_balanced hp).mpr ⟨h1, h2⟩

/-- **Same-bit-length keys are automatically balanced**, hence automatically inside the
canonical window (`in_win = 1`).  This is why a deployed-style pool of two independent
primes of equal bit length never leaves the window ascending scan undefined — and why the
loss it suffers there cannot be blamed on window misses. -/
theorem same_bitlength_in_window {b p q : ℕ} (hb : 1 ≤ b) (hp : 2 ^ (b - 1) ≤ p)
    (hpq : p ≤ q) (hq : q < 2 ^ b) : p * p ≤ p * q ∧ p * q < 2 * (p * p) := by
  have hp0 : 0 < p := lt_of_lt_of_le (Nat.two_pow_pos (b-1)) hp
  have hpow : 2 ^ b = 2 * 2 ^ (b - 1) := by
    conv_lhs => rw [show b = (b - 1) + 1 by omega]
    rw [pow_succ]
    ring
  refine (window_iff_balanced hp0).mpr ⟨hpq, ?_⟩
  omega

theorem exists_semiprime_outside_window :
    ∃ p q : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ q.Prime ∧ p ≤ q ∧ ¬ (p * q < 2 * (p * p)) := by
  refine ⟨3, 7, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num⟩

/-! ## Pool-level totals -/

variable {ι : Type*}

/-- Total ascending touch count over a pool. -/
def totalAsc (s : Finset ι) (a : ℤ) (d : ι → ℤ) : ℤ := ∑ i ∈ s, ascCost a (d i)

/-- Total descending touch count over a pool. -/
def totalDesc (s : Finset ι) (b : ℤ) (d : ι → ℤ) : ℤ := ∑ i ∈ s, descCost b (d i)

    totalAsc s a d = (∑ i ∈ s, d i) - s.card * a + s.card := by
  unfold totalAsc ascCost
  rw [Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
  simp [mul_comm]

    totalDesc s b d = s.card * b - (∑ i ∈ s, d i) + s.card := by
  unfold totalDesc descCost
  rw [Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
  simp [mul_comm]

  rw [totalAsc_eq, totalDesc_eq]; constructor <;> intro h <;> nlinarith [h]

noncomputable def tilt (a b : ℤ) (x : ℤ) : ℝ := ((x : ℝ) - a) / ((b : ℝ) - a)

noncomputable def meanTilt (s : Finset ι) (a b : ℤ) (d : ι → ℤ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ i ∈ s, tilt a b (d i)) / s.card

theorem sum_tilt (s : Finset ι) {a b : ℤ} (hab : a < b) (d : ι → ℤ) :

  have hL : ((b : ℝ) - a) ≠ 0 := by
    have : (a : ℝ) < b := by exact_mod_cast hab
    linarith
  unfold tilt
  rw [← Finset.sum_div, Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
  simp [mul_comm]

    linarith

  rw [sum_tilt s hab d]
  push_cast
  field_simp

  rw [sum_tilt s hab d]
  push_cast
  field_simp
